paragraphs: We have reviewed the general form of the proposed government and the whole mass of power given to it. Next I turn to the particular structure of this government and to how that mass of power is distributed among its parts.

One of the main objections pressed by the more respectable opponents of the Constitution is that it supposedly violates the political maxim that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct. In building the federal government, they say, no attention seems to have been paid to this essential precaution in favor of liberty. The separate departments of power, they say, are distributed and blended in such a way that all symmetry and beauty of form are destroyed, and some essential parts of the edifice are in danger of being crushed by the disproportionate weight of others.

No political truth is certainly of greater intrinsic value, or carries the authority of more enlightened friends of liberty, than the one on which this objection rests. When all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, are gathered into the same hands, whether of one, of a few, or of many, and whether those hands are hereditary, self-appointed, or elected, we may rightly call that the very definition of tyranny. If the federal Constitution were really guilty of gathering power in this way, or of mixing powers in a way that dangerously tended toward it, no further argument would be needed to make everyone condemn the system. I am confident, however, that it will be plain to everyone that the charge cannot be supported, and that the maxim it relies on has been completely misunderstood and misapplied. To form correct ideas on this important subject, we should first investigate in what sense the preservation of liberty requires the three great departments of power to be separate and distinct.

The oracle always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrated Montesquieu. If he is not the author of this invaluable precept in the science of politics, he at least deserves credit for setting it out and recommending it to mankind's attention more effectively than anyone else. Let us try first to determine what he meant on this point.

The British Constitution was to Montesquieu what Homer has been to the writers who teach the rules of epic poetry. Those writers have treated the work of the immortal bard as the perfect model from which the principles and rules of the epic art are to be drawn and by which all similar works are to be judged. In the same way, this great political critic appears to have viewed the Constitution of England as the standard, or, to use his own expression, the mirror of political liberty, and to have stated the characteristic principles of that particular system as if they were elementary truths. So that we do not mistake his meaning, then, let us go back to the source from which the maxim was drawn.

On the slightest look at the British Constitution, we must see that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments are by no means totally separate and distinct from each other. The chief executive is an integral part of the legislative authority. He alone has the prerogative of making treaties with foreign sovereigns, and these treaties, once made, have under certain limitations the force of legislative acts. All the members of the judiciary department are appointed by him. He can remove them on the address of the two Houses of Parliament, and, when he chooses to consult them, they form one of his constitutional councils. One branch of the legislative department also forms a great constitutional council to the executive head. That same branch is the sole holder of judicial power in cases of impeachment, and has the supreme appellate jurisdiction in all other cases. The judges, in turn, are connected with the legislative department closely enough that they often attend and take part in its deliberations, though they are not admitted to a legislative vote.

The reasons on which Montesquieu bases his maxim demonstrate his meaning further. "When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body," says he, "there can be no liberty, because apprehensions may arise lest THE SAME monarch or senate should ENACT tyrannical laws to EXECUTE them in a tyrannical manner." Again: "Were the power of judging joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control, for THE JUDGE would then be THE LEGISLATOR. Were it joined to the executive power, THE JUDGE might behave with all the violence of AN OPPRESSOR." Some of these reasons are explained more fully in other passages. Stated briefly as they are here, they are enough to establish the meaning we have given to this celebrated maxim of this celebrated author.

If we look at the constitutions of the individual States, we find that this axiom has been laid down emphatically and, in some cases, in unqualified terms. Yet in not a single State have the separate departments of power been kept absolutely separate and distinct. New Hampshire, whose constitution was the last one formed, seems to have been fully aware that avoiding any mixture of these departments whatever is impossible and unwise, and it has qualified the doctrine by declaring "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary powers ought to be kept as separate from, and independent of, each other AS THE NATURE OF A FREE GOVERNMENT WILL ADMIT; OR AS IS CONSISTENT WITH THAT CHAIN OF CONNECTION THAT BINDS THE WHOLE FABRIC OF THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE INDISSOLUBLE BOND OF UNITY AND AMITY." Her constitution accordingly mixes these departments in several respects. The Senate, which is a branch of the legislative department, is also a judicial court for the trial of impeachments. The President, who is the head of the executive department, also presides over the Senate and, besides an equal vote in all cases, has a casting vote in case of a tie. The executive head is himself elected each year, in the end, by the legislative department, and his council is chosen each year by the same department and from its members. Several of the officers of state are also appointed by the legislature. And the members of the judiciary department are appointed by the executive department.

The constitution of Massachusetts has shown a sufficient, though less pointed, caution in stating this fundamental article of liberty. It declares "that the legislative department shall never exercise the executive and judicial powers, or either of them; the executive shall never exercise the legislative and judicial powers, or either of them; the judicial shall never exercise the legislative and executive powers, or either of them." This declaration corresponds precisely with the doctrine of Montesquieu as we have explained it, and the plan of the Convention does not violate it at a single point. It goes no further than to forbid any one of the entire departments from exercising the powers of another department. In the very Constitution to which it is prefixed, a partial mixture of powers has been admitted. The chief executive has a qualified negative on the legislative body. The Senate, which is part of the legislature, is a court of impeachment for members of both the executive and the judiciary departments. The members of the judiciary department are appointable by the executive department and removable by the same authority on the address of the two legislative branches. Lastly, a number of the officers of government are appointed each year by the legislative department. Appointment to offices, particularly executive offices, is by its nature an executive function. So the framers of the Constitution have, at least on this last point, violated the rule they set for themselves.

I pass over the constitutions of Rhode Island and Connecticut, because they were formed before the Revolution, and even before the principle under examination had become an object of political attention.

The constitution of New York contains no declaration on this subject, but it appears very clearly to have been framed with an eye to the danger of improperly blending the different departments. It nevertheless gives the chief executive a partial control over the legislative department. What is more, it gives the judiciary department a like control, and it even blends the executive and judiciary departments in the exercise of this control. In its council of appointment, members of the legislative department are associated with the executive authority in appointing officers, both executive and judiciary. And its court for the trial of impeachments and the correction of errors is to consist of one branch of the legislature and the principal members of the judiciary department.

The constitution of New Jersey has blended the different powers of government more than any of those before it. The governor, who is the chief executive, is appointed by the legislature. He is chancellor and ordinary, or surrogate, of the State; he is a member of the Supreme Court of Appeals; and he presides, with a casting vote, over one of the legislative branches. That same legislative branch acts in turn as the governor's executive council and, together with him, forms the Court of Appeals. The members of the judiciary department are appointed by the legislative department and removable by one branch of it on the impeachment of the other.

Under the constitution of Pennsylvania, the president, who is head of the executive department, is elected each year by a vote in which the legislative department predominates. Together with an executive council, he appoints the members of the judiciary department, and he forms a court of impeachment for the trial of all officers, judiciary as well as executive. The judges of the Supreme Court and the justices of the peace seem also to be removable by the legislature, and the executive power of pardoning in certain cases seems to be referred to the same department. The members of the executive council are made EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace throughout the State.

In Delaware, the chief executive is elected each year by the legislative department. The speakers of the two legislative branches are vice-presidents in the executive department. The executive head, with six others appointed three by each of the legislative branches, constitutes the Supreme Court of Appeals, and he joins the legislative department in appointing the other judges. Throughout the States, it appears that members of the legislature may at the same time be justices of the peace. In this State, the members of one branch of the legislature are EX-OFFICIO justices of the peace, and so are the members of the executive council. The principal officers of the executive department are appointed by the legislative department, and one branch of the latter forms a court of impeachments. All officers may be removed on the address of the legislature.

Maryland has adopted the maxim in the most unqualified terms, declaring that the legislative, executive, and judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other. Her constitution nevertheless makes the chief executive appointable by the legislative department, and the members of the judiciary appointable by the executive department.

The language of Virginia on this subject is still more pointed. Her constitution declares, "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct; so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other; nor shall any person exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time, except that the justices of county courts shall be eligible to either House of Assembly." Yet we find not only this express exception for the members of the inferior courts, but also that the chief executive, with his executive council, is appointable by the legislature; that two members of the council are removed every three years at the legislature's pleasure; and that all the principal offices, both executive and judiciary, are filled by the same department. The executive prerogative of pardon, too, is in one case vested in the legislative department.

The constitution of North Carolina declares "that the legislative, executive, and supreme judicial powers of government ought to be forever separate and distinct from each other." At the same time, it gives the legislative department the appointment not only of the executive head but of all the principal officers within both the executive and the judiciary departments.

In South Carolina, the constitution makes the executive office elective by the legislative department. It also gives the legislative department the appointment of the members of the judiciary department, even justices of the peace and sheriffs, and the appointment of officers in the executive department, down to captains in the army and navy of the State.

The constitution of Georgia declares "that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments shall be separate and distinct, so that neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other." Yet we find that the executive department is to be filled by appointments of the legislature, and that the executive prerogative of pardon is to be finally exercised by the same authority. Even justices of the peace are to be appointed by the legislature.

In citing these cases, in which the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments have not been kept totally separate and distinct, I do not wish to be taken as an advocate for the particular organizations of the individual State governments. I am fully aware that, among the many excellent principles they exemplify, they carry strong marks of the haste in which they were framed, and still stronger marks of the inexperience. It is all too obvious that in some cases the fundamental principle under consideration has been violated by too great a mixture, and even an actual consolidation, of the different powers; and that in no case has competent provision been made for maintaining in practice the separation outlined on paper. What I have wished to show is that the charge brought against the proposed Constitution, of violating the sacred maxim of free government, is warranted neither by the real meaning its author gave to that maxim nor by the sense in which it has so far been understood in America. This interesting subject will be resumed in the next paper.
